meta.titre: The Human Eye: parts, image formation and the adjustments to distance and light
meta.sous_theme: Structure of the eye, accommodation and the pupil reflex

source.epreuve_titre: GCE O/L Human Biology past paper (Cameroon)

sections.contenu_markdown: When you walk from the bright sunshine of the school compound into a dim classroom, you can hardly see at first, and then the details slowly appear. The eye has changed the size of its pupil, and it also changes the shape of its lens whenever you look from the board to your exercise book. Questions on the eye are common in Human Biology: you may be asked to draw and label it, to give the function of each part, or to explain what happens when we look at near objects or in bright light.

items: Light travels in straight lines and is bent (refracted) when it passes from one transparent material into another.
A receptor detects a stimulus, and impulses are carried by nerves to the brain.
Circular muscles form a ring around an opening, and radial muscles run outwards like the spokes of a wheel.

sections.titre: Structure and functions of the human eye
sections.contenu_markdown:
### Parts of the eye

| Part | Function |
|---|---|
| Sclera | Tough white outer coat; protects the eye and keeps its shape |
| Cornea | Transparent front of the eye; bends light most strongly |
| Choroid | Dark layer rich in blood vessels; absorbs stray light and feeds the retina |
| Retina | Inner layer holding the light receptors (rods and cones) |
| Iris | Coloured ring of muscle; controls the size of the pupil |
| Pupil | Hole in the centre of the iris through which light enters |
| Lens | Transparent, elastic and curved outwards on both sides; focuses light onto the retina |
| Ciliary muscle and suspensory ligaments | Hold the lens and change its shape |
| Aqueous humour | Watery fluid in front of the lens; keeps the shape of the front of the eye and nourishes the cornea and lens |
| Vitreous humour | Clear jelly behind the lens; keeps the eyeball in shape and holds the retina in place |
| Fovea (yellow spot) | Part of the retina with the most cones; gives the sharpest, coloured vision |
| Blind spot | Place where the optic nerve leaves; no receptors, so no vision |
| Optic nerve | Carries impulses from the retina to the brain |

### How an image is formed

Light is refracted by the cornea (most strongly) and by the lens, and a small, upside-down (inverted) image forms on the retina. The receptors send impulses along the optic nerve to the brain, which interprets the image the right way up.

variantes.nom: Focusing on near and distant objects (accommodation)
variantes.quand_utiliser: When a question asks how the eye focuses on objects at different distances.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Near object: the ciliary muscles contract, the suspensory ligaments become slack, the lens becomes thicker and rounder and bends light more. Distant object: the ciliary muscles relax, the suspensory ligaments are pulled tight, the lens becomes thinner and flatter and bends light less. In both cases the image is focused on the retina.

variantes.nom: Response to bright and dim light (pupil reflex)
variantes.quand_utiliser: When a question asks what happens to the pupil, or why the eye adjusts to light intensity.
variantes.contenu_markdown: In bright light the circular muscles of the iris contract and the radial muscles relax, so the pupil becomes smaller, less light enters, and the retina is protected. In dim light the radial muscles contract and the circular muscles relax, so the pupil becomes larger and more light enters. This is a reflex: the receptors in the retina send impulses along the optic nerve to the brain, and motor impulses go to the muscles of the iris.

variantes.nom: Rods, cones and drawing the eye
variantes.quand_utiliser: When a question asks about colour vision or dim light, or asks for a labelled diagram.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Cones work in bright light, detect colour and give detail; they are most numerous at the fovea. Rods work in dim light and give black and white vision. When you draw the eye, use a sharp pencil, make the drawing large, use clear continuous lines, draw label lines with a ruler that touch the part and do not cross, and write a title.

sections.enonce_markdown: A student looks up from her notebook at a bird sitting in a tree outside the classroom window. Explain the changes in her eyes that allow her to see the bird clearly. *(5 marks)*

etapes.justification: The eyes change from a near object to a distant one, so the process is accommodation.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The eye must change from focusing on a near object to focusing on a **distant** object.

etapes.justification: The lens is controlled by the ciliary muscles.
The ligaments hold the lens and change tension when the muscles change.
The shape of the lens decides how strongly light is bent.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The lens becomes **thinner and flatter**, so it bends light less.

etapes.justification: The aim is a sharp image on the retina.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Light from the bird is focused as a sharp image on the retina.

sections.conclusion_markdown: **Model answer.** When she looks at the distant bird, the ciliary muscles relax and the suspensory ligaments are pulled tight. The lens is pulled thinner and flatter, so it bends light rays less, and light from the bird is focused as a sharp image on the retina.

items.erreur_markdown: "The lens does most of the bending of light."
items.pourquoi_faux: Most refraction takes place at the cornea. The lens adjusts the focus.
items.correction_markdown: The cornea bends light most; the lens makes fine adjustments.

items.erreur_markdown: "In bright light the pupil becomes bigger."
items.pourquoi_faux: A large pupil would let too much light in and could damage the retina.
items.correction_markdown: In bright light the pupil becomes **smaller**.

items.erreur_markdown: "Cones work in dim light, and rods detect colour."
items.pourquoi_faux: The functions are the other way round.
items.correction_markdown: **Cones**: bright light and colour. **Rods**: dim light and black and white.

items.erreur_markdown: "To look at a near object, the ciliary muscles relax and the lens becomes thinner."
items.pourquoi_faux: This describes looking at a distant object.
items.correction_markdown: Near object: ciliary muscles **contract** and the lens becomes **thicker**.

items.erreur_markdown: "The image on the retina is the right way up."
items.pourquoi_faux: The image on the retina is upside down; the brain interprets it the right way up.

items.enonce_markdown: Name the part of the eye that: (a) controls the amount of light entering; (b) contains the light receptors; (c) carries impulses to the brain; (d) is the clear jelly behind the lens; (e) is the dark layer that absorbs stray light; (f) is the transparent front part where most refraction takes place.

Student A is reading outside in bright sunlight and student B is sitting in a dim room. (a) Compare the size of their pupils. (b) Name the muscles of the iris that are contracted in each case. (c) Explain why the difference is useful to each student. (d) Name the cells in the retina that student B uses to see.
items.solution_markdown: (a) A's pupils are **small** and B's are **large**. (b) A: the circular muscles are contracted. B: the radial muscles are contracted. (c) For A, a small pupil lets in less light and protects the retina from damage. For B, a large pupil lets in more light so that the dim object can be seen. (d) **Rods**, which work in dim light.

items.enonce_markdown: A student measures the pupil of a model eye. The diameter is 2 mm in bright light and 6 mm in dim light. Use area $= \pi r^2$ with $\pi = 3.14$. (a) Calculate the area of the pupil in each case. (b) How many times larger is the area in dim light? (c) If the light intensity were the same, how many times more light would enter the eye through the larger pupil? (d) Explain how this helps vision in dim light, and name the muscles that make the pupil larger.
items.solution_markdown: (a) Bright light: $r = 1\ \text{mm}$, so $A = 3.14 \times 1^2 = 3.14\ \text{mm}^2$. Dim light: $r = 3\ \text{mm}$, so $A = 3.14 \times 3^2 = 28.26\ \text{mm}^2$. (b) $\frac{28.26}{3.14} = 9$, so **9 times larger**. (c) The amount of light entering is proportional to the area of the pupil, so **9 times more light**. (d) More light reaches the retina, so the rods can be stimulated and the dim object can be seen. The **radial muscles** of the iris contract to enlarge the pupil.

items_markdown: Cornea: most refraction. Lens: fine focusing. Retina: receptors. Iris: controls the pupil. Choroid: absorbs stray light and feeds the retina.
The retinal image is small and upside down; the brain interprets it the right way up.
Near object: ciliary muscles contract, ligaments slack, lens thicker. Distant object: ciliary muscles relax, ligaments tight, lens thinner.
Bright light: circular muscles contract, pupil small. Dim light: radial muscles contract, pupil large.
Cones give colour and detail in bright light (most at the fovea); rods work in dim light. The blind spot has no receptors.
